claims.text: The disparate stress–strain and thermoelastic behaviors of HfNbTaTiZr arise from internal stresses generated by thermal-expansion mismatch during thermal cycling.
Differential expansion across microstructural regions alters dislocation mobility in HfNbTaTiZr.
The proposed initial state is homogenized, conventionally cast HfNbTaTiZr.
Controlled thermal cycling between 293 K and 1250 °C, with varied heating and cooling rates, is the proposed intervention.
Distinct microstructural regions, including grain-boundary regions and differently oriented grains, undergo differential thermal expansion.
Differential thermal expansion between microstructural regions produces internal thermal stresses.
Internal thermal stresses modify dislocation glide and climb during thermal cycling.
The resulting stress fields can locally impede or facilitate dislocation movement.
Changes in dislocation movement caused by internal stress influence creep behavior.
Changes in dislocation movement caused by internal stress influence hardness.
Changes in dislocation movement caused by internal stress influence elastic moduli.
Controlled thermal cycling will alter yield strength relative to standard air-cooled samples.
Controlled thermal cycling will reduce high-temperature creep rates relative to standard air-cooled samples.
Controlled thermal cycling will shift elastic moduli relative to standard air-cooled samples.
The proposed mechanism is expected to govern behavior from 293 K to 1250 °C under low applied stress.
Outside the specified temperature range, phase transitions may overshadow thermal-expansion effects.
Under high applied stress, excessive plastic deformation may overshadow thermal-expansion effects.
The magnitude and spatial distribution of internal stress depend on microstructural heterogeneity and processing history.

contradictions.description: The stated validity condition is low applied stress, but the proposed comparison includes full stress–strain curves and yield-strength measurements, which necessarily extend beyond a low-stress regime. The hypothesis does not distinguish which measurements must remain at low stress.
